newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: NZ Treasurer eyes policy easing on pension vote.
newsitem.headline: NZ Treasurer eyes policy easing on pension vote.

text.p: New Zealand Deputy Prime Minister and Treasurer Winston Peters indicated on Wednesday he expected the Reserve Bank of New Zealand to ease monetary policy in 1998 if a referendum on a compulsory pension scheme was successful.

Peters said if the savings plan was accepted by voters in a September referendum and implemented from July next year the Reserve Bank would have to look at a more accommodating policy to help the economy cope with the effect of higher savings and lower consumption.

"I'd expect a countervailing response to there being somewhat less money in the economy as a result of the savings strategy," Peters told reporters when asked if the Reserve Bank should ease policy if the vote was successful.
The Reserve Bank had not included the savings plan in its forecasts and would therefore have to adjust to the short term slowing effect of higher savings.
This expected easing would mean the savings plan would not change the government's forecast growth path, he later told Reuters Financial Television (RFTV) in an interview.
"We'd an expect an (RBNZ) accommodation of that (referendum) result which should not have any deleterious effect on our growth strategy," Peters said.

Peters was speaking after an address to a Trans-Tasman Business Circle in Sydney, where he also said the New Zealand dollar may fall further than the five percent he said it had already fallen since February.
The New Zealand dollar dropped to US$0.6734/39 by the close from its US$0.6758/65 opening on Peters' comments.
Short-term interest rates also rose to partly compensate for the stronger dollar.
The Reserve Bank targets a combination of the New Zealand dollar and interest rates called the Monetary Conditions Index.
Unless rates move in the opposite direction to the currency, the index moves too far outside from the RBNZ's target range.
As it was, the index fell to 61 points below the RBNZ's target level from 44 points below earlier on Wednesday.
This took it outside the 50 point variation range the bank has said it would tolerate.
Peters released a white paper on Monday outlining the structure of a compulsory superannuation scheme that would be put to a national referendum in September.
The plan requires all earners to contribute three percent of their income to the scheme to build up about NZ$120,000.
That lump sum would then be used to buy an annuity after retirement equal to the current state pension.

Peters said the government could not afford to continue with its current state-funded superannuation system because of an impending surge in the numbers of elderly people and the lower proportion of working age people to pay their pensions.
Peters said it would be a tough battle to convince people to vote for the scheme, given opinion polls showed a majority against the proposal.
But he said a no vote would inevitably mean either higher taxes, lower spending or a higher debt, none of which were sustainable.
Peters also later said budget forecasts of surpluses of over NZ$1 billion (US$674 million) a year for the next two years remained on track despite surprisingly weak GDP data released late last month.
"I think there's been a turnaround even since the (June 27) budget in business confidence," he said.
Peters said the recent fall in the New Zealand dollar would also help the current account deficit, which has risen sharply in the last year because of the stronger currency in 1996.
